title: Delegates and lambdas
cards/0/title: A variable that holds a method
cards/0/body: A delegate is an object that holds a reference to a method. You can pass it to another method, put it in a list, or call it later.
cards/1/body:
Func<…, TResult> — takes arguments and returns a result (the last type parameter is the result type).
Action<…> — returns nothing.
Predicate<T> — returns bool.
cards/2/q: Match the signature to the delegate
cards/3/title: A lambda is a method without a name
cards/3/body: You can write a method right where you need it: x => x * 2. The compiler infers the types from where the lambda is passed.
cards/4/q: A delegate that takes a string and returns bool
cards/4/explain: Predicate<string> would work too, but there are two gaps here — Func<string, bool>.
cards/5/body: Delegates are multicast: += adds a method to the invocation list. Calling the delegate runs them all in order. If it returns a value, you get the result of the last one.
cards/6/explain: Both run, but you get the result of the last one in the list.
cards/7/q: How is Action different from Func?
cards/7/options/0: Action returns nothing, Func returns a result
cards/7/explain: Func<int> returns an int; Action<int> takes an int and returns nothing.
cards/8/q: Which are true about delegates? Select all.
cards/8/options/0: A delegate is an object on the heap
cards/8/options/1: You can pass a delegate to a method
cards/8/options/2: += adds a method to the invocation list
cards/8/options/3: A lambda cannot be a delegate
cards/8/explain: A lambda is exactly what turns into a delegate (or an expression tree).
